Exploring Factors of Price, Age, and Region of Origin as Predictors of Online Community Wine Ratings
Key Takeaways
Within both the red and white wine models, higher prices, a lower age, and production in an Old World Country were associated with greater odds of having a High rating
Effects of price, age, and region of origin were stronger in white wine model

Simpson’s Paradox explained with age variable since price mediates effect of age on Rating; challenges assumptions that higher price and older age equates to higher rating, reveals a more nuanced relationship.
Generalizability
Website: Wine ratings from one specific website by a unique user base; unable to generalize our results beyond the Vivino website

Time: Since data was collected 4 years ago, may be differences if the same model were to be fitted with current data (majority of wines in the dataset were produced in the last 4 years); generalizability of our results is thus limited to the short-term of the time of data collection
Unable to make any causal inferences from the data as there was no manipulation of variables or random assignment procedures with the data
Limitations
Uncertainty with data collection method from Vivino prevents us from being able to assume random selection and validly interpret results

Bias: geographic bias due to the nature of Vivino website being most popular in North America and Europe (location of its main offices are in Denmark and the United States); selection bias due to the most popular and available wines being viewed and rated more frequently
Future Research Directions

Future directions for research could involve the inclusion of more wine types, more total wines, and perhaps deeper dives into the regions within countries and signature wines (e.g., Cabernet Sauvignon vs Pinot Noir)
Adding more variables (e.g., chemical profiles, winery) would be useful to strengthen the model and examine more detailed differences in wine ratings based on specific attributes of different wines
Setting baseline point for “High/Low” rating could be adjusted to different percentiles beyond 50th percentile to see if differences emerge

Source Website
Gathered data from Vivino.com, world’s largest wine marketplace containing reviews from community members

Found subset from Kaggle file containing data points for 33,605 different wine bottles; includes five smaller sub-datasets with variables for each type of wine: Red, White, Rose, Sparkling, and Varieties
Modeled red/white wine datasets; (nr = 8666, nw = 3764)
Both datasets include variables name, country, region, winery, numerical rating (1-5 scale), number of ratings, price (in Euros), and year of production
Data Wrangling

Of 30 countries included in each dataset, 20 countries were classified as Old World Wine Countries (European wines, e.g., France, Italy); other 10 countries were New World Wine Countries (e.g., Australia, United States)
For binomial logistic analysis, ratings equal to/above median rating were labeled as “high” rating, ratings below median rating were labeled as “low” rating (med(r) = 3.9, med(w) = 3.8)
Price was transformed to Log(Price) due to significant right skew of price observations, since a few wines were very expensive (range: €3.6 - €3410.8)
Year was calculated as years since 2020: year in which data was collected
Model Building
Logistic regression model log P(Y = 1)/1 − P(Y = 1) = 𝛽0 + β1x1 + β2x2 + β3x3 for both red and white wine datasets
With our selected variables plugged in, we obtain the model Rating = 𝛽0 + 𝛽1 Age + 𝛽2 log(Price)+ 𝛽3 World
Research Question 1: Are fluctuations in year and price of wine associated with a higher wine rating?
Research Question 2: Does the origin country of wine (Old World vs New World) impact its rating?
Significance of Current Research
We seek to build upon the previous research on factors affecting wine quality evaluations, through investigating a large dataset of wine ratings which includes various countries
Older wines have been to shown to be associated with an “increased fruit flavor, lower astringent and reductive flavor” which all lead to a higher wine quality (Echave et al., 2021)

Wine experts and traders exhibit implicit biases favoring Old World wines (e.g., French and Swiss) over New World wines (e.g., Brazilian and Argentinean), often rating the former more favorably and describing them with more positive sensory language (Chauvin et al., 2024)

Country of origin influences wine traders’ mental representations, with traditional Old World producers benefiting from strong country images, while New World producers like Argentina face challenges when introducing wines that deviate from expected national styles (Rodrigues et al., 2020)

Old World consumers rely more heavily on country-of-origin information in shaping their perception and categorization of wines, while New World consumers focus more on the sensory qualities of the wine regardless of its origin (Valentin et al., 2021)

Research can shed light on factors that influence wine ratings, a key component in consumer decision-making and market value; by identifying how variables like price, age, and region of origin relate to perceived wine quality, the study can offer insights for both wine producers and consumers.
Hypothesis: Older, more expensive, and “Old World” wines will have higher odds of being rated more highly
